questions.question: A proof splits into three cases: "n is divisible by 3", "n leaves remainder 1 when divided by 3", and "n is odd". What is the main problem?
options: Proofs by cases may only use two cases
The cases overlap, which is never allowed
Divisibility cannot be used as a case condition
The cases are not exhaustive, since n = 2 fits none of them
questions.explanation: Cases may overlap and there can be any number of them, but together they must cover every possibility. n = 2 is not divisible by 3, leaves remainder 2, and is even, so no case covers it.

questions.question: In the six-people proof, why does choosing a single person P and counting P's friends work so well?
options: Because P has 5 relationships, so P has at least 3 friends or at least 3 strangers
Because P is friends with everyone
Because every group of 3 people must include P
Because P can be chosen to have exactly 3 friends
questions.explanation: Five relationships cannot split as 2 friends and 2 strangers or fewer, so one side has at least 3. That forces a group Q, R, S, and the sub-cases on their relationships finish the proof. P can be anyone. We don't get to choose P's friendships.

questions.question: When is strong induction clearly more convenient than ordinary induction?
options: When the claim is about real numbers
When a size-n problem splits into smaller pieces whose sizes are not just n - 1
When there is no base case
When the claim is an existence statement
questions.explanation: Strong induction lets you assume P(k) for every k below n. That is exactly what you need when a split, like the unstacking game or a beat ordering, creates pieces of unpredictable smaller size. It still needs a starting case, and it works over the natural numbers.

questions.question: In the beat-ordering proof, a pivot team T beat every other team, so W (the teams that beat T) is empty. What happens?
options: The proof fails because W must be non-empty
We must pick a different pivot
The line-up is just T followed by a beat ordering of L, and the proof still works
T must go last in the line-up
questions.explanation: An empty group has a trivially valid (empty) ordering. T goes first, and T beat the first team in L. The proof never needed W or L to be non-empty.
